readerTitle: The food hall owner who never cooks
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑, 푸드홀, 미용실 예약 앱) + 일반적 관찰 (쇼핑몰, 농산물 시장)
insight: 제품과 플랫폼의 차이는 무엇을 파느냐가 아니라 누가 가치를 만드느냐다. 플랫폼의 일은 남이 성공하도록 돕는 것이다.
misconception: 플랫폼은 그냥 더 큰 제품이다. 손님을 늘리려면 내가 더 좋은 것을 직접 만들어야 한다.

sources.text: 제품과 플랫폼의 구분은 경영 전략의 일반 개념 (플랫폼 비즈니스, 양면 시장 문헌)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 레스토랑, 푸드홀, 미용실 예약 앱은 모두 가상 사례입니다. 구체적인 수치나 실제 기업명은 쓰지 않았습니다.
쇼핑몰, 농산물 시장, 앱 마켓, 온라인 마켓플레이스가 입점자에게 임대료나 수수료를 받는다는 설명은 일반적인 관찰입니다. 특정 기업의 수수료율은 언급하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The food hall owner who never cooks
body: Two food businesses sit on the same street. One is a restaurant. Its owner hires the chef, writes the menu and cooks every plate.
Next door is a food hall with twelve stalls. Its owner hasn't cooked a single dish. Both are busy. They grow in completely different ways.

image.label: A restaurant kitchen next to a food hall with many stalls
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽은 셰프 한 명이 요리하는 작은 레스토랑, 오른쪽은 서로 다른 간판의 노점 여러 개가 모인 푸드홀. 푸드홀 주인은 가운데에서 클립보드만 들고 서 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: Weekdays are slow at the food hall.
body: You own the food hall. Weekends are packed, but weekday lunches are quiet. Some vendors say they may not renew their leases.

options.text: Hire a well-known chef to open your own house stall
options.feedback: A star stall could draw a crowd. But you'd be competing with your own vendors, and their success is what pays your rent.

options.text: Help vendors win weekdays: a shared prep kitchen, a lunch deal for nearby offices, cheap short leases for new pop-ups
options.feedback: You spend money on tools and traffic instead of food. If vendors do better, more of them stay and new ones want in.

options.text: Cut prices at your drinks bar to pull people in
options.feedback: Cheap drinks may bring a few people, but it trims your own margin and does little for the vendors who are thinking of leaving.

cards.title: Same street, different engines.
body: The restaurant grows by cooking more and better. The food hall grows by making it easier for **other people** to cook and sell.

breakdown.label: Restaurant: who makes the value
breakdown.detail: Your chef, your menu, your plates

breakdown.label: Food hall: who makes the value
Food hall: how it earns
breakdown.detail: A share of what vendors make

cards.title: Products vs platforms
body: A **product** is something you make and sell. You create the value, and you control its quality.
A **platform** is a shared base that lets others create value and reach customers. You provide the space, tools, rules and crowd. Your value is mostly the sum of what your partners make.
So the question isn't how big you are. It's *who makes the thing customers come for*.

image.label: One hand holding a dish vs a stage with many performers
image.brief: 두 칸 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Product": 사업자가 직접 만든 접시 하나를 손님에게 건넴. 오른쪽 "Platform": 사업자가 만든 넓은 무대 위에서 여러 판매자가 손님과 거래함. 무대 바닥에 "Space, tools, rules, crowd" 라벨.

cards.title: Platforms are older than apps.
body: Shopping malls rent space to shops. Farmers' markets give growers a place, a day and a crowd. App stores and online marketplaces do the same for developers and sellers.
Each one earns rent or a cut. And each one wins only when the people on it win. That changes the job: less making, more **setting rules, building tools and bringing customers**.

cards.title: Platforms are harder than they look.
body: An empty food hall attracts no vendors, and no vendors means no diners. Starting a platform means solving that chicken-and-egg problem, often by first acting like a product yourself.
You also give up control. One dirty stall can hurt every stall. A platform needs rules and the will to enforce them.
Most businesses should be great products first. Becoming a platform is a choice, not a promotion.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app for salons.
body: Your app handles appointments for hair salons. Users keep asking for more: stock tracking, payroll, text reminders. Three outside developers ask if they can build add-ons that plug into your app.

options.text: Say no and build every requested feature yourself
options.feedback: You keep full control of quality. But your small team becomes the bottleneck, and users wait a long time for features others could build.

options.text: Keep booking excellent, and open a reviewed way for developers to plug in
options.feedback: Your core product stays strong while others add value you'd never get to. The cost is new work: rules, reviews and support for partners.

options.text: Launch a full add-on store now and pause work on booking
options.feedback: Developers only come if many salons use you. Neglect the core product and you may end up with a store and nobody shopping.

cards.title: Ask who makes the value: you, or the people you host.
body: A product grows by making more and better. A platform grows by helping others succeed on it. Each needs different work and different measures.
**Try it today:** list what your customers come to you for. Mark which parts you make yourself and which parts someone else could make on top of you.
